definition: The California Consumer Privacy Act is a state law that gives California residents rights over their personal information, including the right to know, delete, and opt-out of sale.
metaDescription: Learn about the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) - a privacy law giving California residents control over their personal data and information.
simpleExplanation: The CCPA is California's privacy law that lets residents control their personal data. You can ask companies what info they have about you, request deletion, and stop them from selling it to others.
whyItMatters: It gives consumers significant control over their personal data and forces companies to be transparent about data collection practices. Even non-California residents benefit as many companies apply CCPA standards globally.
technicalDetail: Applies to businesses with $25M+ revenue, 50,000+ consumer records, or 50%+ revenue from selling personal information. Requires clear privacy policies, consumer request mechanisms, and opt-out links. Violations can result in fines up to $7,500 per violation.

examples.explanation: A California resident can request that an online retailer provide all personal information collected about them, including purchase history, browsing data, and any third parties it was shared with.
A user can ask a social media platform to delete all their personal information, including posts, messages, and behavioral data used for advertising targeting.
Consumers can demand that data brokers stop selling their personal information to advertisers and remove their profiles from commercial databases.
